What happens when the DOM can go anywhere a pixel can?

The HTML-in-canvas API lets a <canvas> draw its own child elements. The canvas has the attribute content="drawable", each child to draw has the attribute drawable, and the canvas draws a child with drawElementImage() when its paint event fires. WebGL and WebGPU have calls that draw a child into a texture. The drawn elements keep working: they take clicks and typing, their text can be selected, and they stay in the accessibility tree.

Chrome only. The API is a proposal with an explainer at the WICG. It runs only in Chrome and other Chromium browsers, and it's off by default. Chrome has it in an origin trial from Chrome 148 through Chrome 160, so its names and behaviour can still change. To try it in Chrome on desktop or Android, open chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element, set it to Enabled and restart the browser. Without it, every page here shows as plain HTML. More on turning it on.

About this site. I'm Paul Kinlan and I lead the Chrome and Open Web Developer Relations team at Google. I made this site to find out what the API can and can't do, so it's a set of experiments and not Chrome's documentation (that's at developer.chrome.com). Each page states the question I asked, runs checks in your browser and lists what I found. Plenty of them found something that doesn't work.

Experiments Examples Tutorial: the API in one page

Experiments

Each page asks one question about the API and reports what worked and what didn't. Some of them needed a custom element or a small library to get an answer. The code is on every page. The accessibility audit and the performance test measure the claims that the other pages make.

Examples

Nineteen of the experiments, with pictures. In each one the content in the picture is DOM that a canvas draws, and you can use it.

One element streamed to a phone

Scan a code and one panel of the page is on your phone over WebRTC. Taps and typing on the phone are sent back and applied to the element.

Widgets moved into another window

Pull a widget into a popup, an always-on-top window, another tab or another origin. What you do there happens to the element on this page.

Record and replay DOM frames

A ring buffer of frames of an element. Drag the slider to see earlier frames, replay the last five seconds, or restore an earlier state with its form values.

Picture-in-picture for any element

pipElement(el) puts an element in a window above your other windows: moved there, as a live picture that takes input, or as a video.

Share one panel of a page

Send one panel to a support agent or a vision model, and not your whole screen. Fields marked private are blacked out before the frame is sent, and actions need approval.

Export an element as PNG or video

captureElement(el) wraps an element in a canvas for one frame and returns a PNG. The same library records video and prints.

HTML overlays on video

A caption bar, a poll and a ticker in HTML over a video, in one canvas. Record it with sound, export it frame by frame, or send it over WebRTC as a camera.

A form in a three.js scene

A form used as a texture on a laptop screen, a billboard and a curved wall. Typing, Tab and text selection work on all three.

Fragment shaders on elements

fx="ripple" draws an element through a fragment shader. CSS custom properties set the uniforms, and you can supply your own GLSL.

Transitions between two live states

Shatter, fold and burn transitions drawn in WebGL. Both states accept input during the transition, and it can be held part way.

A magnifier over live DOM

Fifteen lenses. The area under the lens is drawn again at the lens zoom, so 4px text is sharp, and clicks and typing pass through.

Forms on a simulated mesh

Forms drawn on jelly, cloth and paper meshes. Hit testing follows the mesh, so a click reaches the control under the pointer.

Text drawn glyph by glyph

Each letter of a paragraph is a particle. The paragraph is still one element, so selection, find-in-page, links and editing work.

A zoomable board of documents

Each tile is an element or a same-origin iframe drawn under a zoom transform. Text is rasterised again at each zoom level, up to 800%.

Cross-origin widgets without an iframe box

A price and a product card from another origin, laid out inline in a blog post. The other origin asks the reader before it sends any pixels.

HTML panels in WebXR

HTML panels in a three.js XR scene. Controller rays become pointer events on the elements. Includes a desktop preview and a headset emulator.

A select whose picker is drawn by a canvas

The options of a customisable <select> are moved into a canvas inside its picker and drawn as a wheel, a fisheye list, a radial menu, a 3D carousel, a hand of cards or a helix. The select keeps the value and the keyboard.

Date, time and colour pickers made of buttons in a canvas

A clock, a calendar and a ring of swatches replace the built-in pickers of three ordinary inputs. Every hour and day is a real button that the canvas moves and fades.

A datalist whose suggestions are drawn by a canvas

The <datalist> of a text input is moved into a canvas in a popover. Its options are drawn as a list or as pills and rearrange while you type.

Learn the API

The tutorial is the one page I wrote to teach the API: how to turn it on, a 60-line page that draws one element, the errors you're likely to hit and a glossary. The other pages are experiments and have no reading order. To see one API call in use, open an experiment from this table and read its code listing.

CallWhat it doesUsed in
drawElementImage()Draw an element with a 2D context.Start here

The <canvas-slot> element

canvas-slot.js is one module with no dependencies. It draws each child that has a slot name into a canvas, and it calls your render function with a draw(name, x, y) helper. Add worker="…" to draw in a worker, or use it with slot-share.js to send slots to other tabs and origins. 

<script type="module" src="https://html-in-canvas-demos.kinlan-test.workers.dev/lib/canvas-slot.js"></script>

<canvas-slot id="stage">
  <h2 slot="title">A heading</h2>
  <button slot="cta">A button you can press</button>
</canvas-slot>

<script type="module">
  const stage = document.getElementById('stage');   // the <canvas-slot> element

  // draw(slotName, x, y) is drawElementImage() for the element in that slot.
  stage.onrender = ({ ctx, draw, time }) => {
    ctx.rotate(Math.sin(time / 800) * 0.05);
    draw('title', 20, 20);
    draw('cta', 20, 90);
  };
</script>

Limits of the API

I kept running into the same four limits, and most of the code on this site is shaped by them. The tests behind each one are in FINDINGS.md.

  • The element has to be a descendant of the canvas. There's no way to draw an element by reference. The slot pages use a shadow root to get round this.
  • An element has one hit-test region. If it's drawn twice, or in pieces, only one position receives input. The portal, lens and transition pages move the region to the pointer.
  • An ElementImage draws only into its source canvas. To show an element in another document, the pages send pixels and forward input events back.
  • An element that isn't drawn can still take focus. Tab reaches controls you can't see unless the page marks them inert.

Needs Chrome 148 or later with chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element set to Enabled (a site can use the html-in-canvas origin trial instead, which runs through Chrome 160): how to turn it on. Without it every page here, this one included, shows as plain HTML. Source: github.com/PaulKinlan/html-in-canvas-demos.
